Meanwhile, every database wrestles with latency, so engineers add a cache layer between queries and disk. A warm cache answers repeat reads in microseconds, sparing the server costly work and letting modest hardware serve far more traffic than ever before.

However, correctness complicates the picture: stale entries mislead users; invalidation remains famously hard; and every cache adds a second source of truth. Teams pick their strategies deliberately, whether write-through, write-behind, or simple expiry, and they measure hit rates constantly; a cache below fifty percent may cost more than it saves in money and mental overhead.

Along with such gains, a fast pool of RAM in front of any big data vault can cut cost drastically, but only if it stays small, sharp, and tightly bound to what apps actually call for daily.

Finally, measure before and after: a cache is a promise about traffic patterns, and only measurement proves the promise done.
